text: - val surgical debulking in those with suboptimal debulking at primary surgery,3,18 and intraperitoneal chemotherapy in those with minimal residual disease after primary sur- gery.3,19-21 The use of neoadjuvant chemotherapy is con- troversial,3 although it has been suggested to reduce mor- bidity and permit subsequent surgical debulking, and studies of this strategy followed by interval surgery are un- derway.18,19 In patients with recurrent disease, the choice of therapy de- pends on the time since initial therapy and the drugs used.1,3,22 Relapse occurring more than 6 months after ini- tial therapy is potentially platinum-sensitive and may be re-treated with the initial therapy. In patients who are po- tentially not sensitive to platinum derivatives, paclitaxel may be used if it was not used previously. Combining pa- clitaxel with platinum chemotherapy may further improve survival in patients who are platinum-sensitive.23 Other drugs with activity include topotecan, liposomal doxoru- bicin, altretamine, capecitabine, cyclophosphamide, do- cetaxel, epirubicin, oral etoposide, gemcitabine, ifosfa- mide, irinotecan, tamoxifen, and vinorelbine.3,18,19,22,24 Bevacizumab is also active.3,19 The monoclonal antibodies oregovomab and pemtumomab are under investigation, as are ovarian cancer vaccines.25 Some success has been re- ported using high-dose chemotherapy followed by autolo- gous stem cell transplantation,26 although an improvement in survival has not been shown.3,18 Prophylaxis. The identification of genes conferring an in- herited predisposition to ovarian cancer, and the difficulty in identifying the disease and its poor prognosis has led to increased interest in prevention. Oral contraceptives are known to be protective in the general population, and there is growing evidence that women with mutation of the BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene might benefit similarly (see Ova- ry, under Carcinogenicity in Hormonal Contraceptives, p.2061). Prophylactic oophorectomy may be considered in women with BRCA1 mutations after child-bearing or at age 35 years.27,28 The risk/benefit ratio of this procedure is not known, and a few women who undergo this procedure subsequently develop a primary peritoneal cancer. Ovarian germ-cell cancers account for less than 3% of ovarian cancers and typically occur in women aged 20 to 30 years. Unlike epithelial ovarian cancer, most patients present with early disease, and even in advanced disease, combination chemotherapy can be curative.3,29 Conserva- tive fertility-sparing surgery is the main therapy.
